lead: A dye streak in a glass pipe is the simplest test of flow character. At low speed the dye stays a thin straight line: laminar flow, where fluid layers slide past each other. At high speed the dye breaks into swirls and clouds: turbulent flow, where particles mix across the pipe. The Reynolds number Re tells you which regime to expect before you open the valve. It is used to size water mains, oil pipelines, blood-flow models and chemical reactors.
prereq: You need: viscosity and density from Unit 1, and the laminar–turbulent classification from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Reynolds' apparatus makes the flow pattern visible. A constant-head tank holds water at a fixed level, so the pressure at the pipe inlet does not change with time. A glass tube of diameter D is connected to the tank. A control valve at the outlet sets the mean velocity V. A small dye reservoir feeds a fine needle at the tube entrance. The dye is a coloured liquid with nearly the same density as water. A measuring jar collects the outflow so you can find discharge Q and then V = Q / (πD²/4).

items: Fill the tank and let the water settle.
Open the valve slightly until water flows steadily.
Release a thin dye thread into the glass tube.
Record the dye shape and measure Q with the jar and a stopwatch.
Raise the valve opening in small steps and repeat.

blocks.text: The flow regime is fixed by one dimensionless group.

blocks.where: ρ is density in kg/m³; V is mean velocity in m/s; D is pipe diameter in m; μ is dynamic viscosity in Pa·s; ν = μ/ρ is kinematic viscosity in m²/s.

blocks.text: Re has no units. The same pipe can be laminar or turbulent: increase V or D and Re rises; increase viscosity and Re falls. For pipe flow, common textbook values are lower critical Re ≈ 2000 and upper critical Re ≈ 4000. Below 2000 the flow is laminar. Between 2000 and 4000 it is transitional; some syllabi call this the critical zone. Above 4000 it is turbulent. The exact switch depends on entrance disturbances, vibration and surface finish, so treat 2000 and 4000 as guides, not sharp walls.

At low Re the dye thread stays straight for the whole length of the tube. A particle of dye stays in its own layer; this is laminar flow. The velocity profile is a paraboloid: zero at the wall and maximum at the centre. The Hagen–Poiseuille result for this profile is in Chapter 4.2. As Re enters the critical zone, the dye line starts to wave. Small disturbances grow. At high Re the dye mixes across the pipe within a short distance and forms a blurred cloud. This is turbulent flow. The time-averaged velocity profile is flatter in the middle and steeper near the wall, because eddies carry momentum across the pipe. The wall layer still has low speed, but the core moves almost as a block. The dye test is qualitative; Re is the quantitative test. Use Re to classify, then use the correct friction law in later sections.

figure.caption: The constant-head tank drives water through a glass tube; dye from the reservoir makes the flow visible, and the valve sets the velocity. At low Re the dye thread is straight; at high Re it breaks into a cloud.

spec.title: Reynolds experiment
spec.aria: A constant-head tank sends water through a glass tube where dye is injected; a valve controls flow into a measuring jar.

examples.question: Water (ν = 1.0×10⁻⁶ m²/s) flows through a 50 mm diameter glass pipe. The mean velocity is 0.06 m/s. Find Re and classify the flow. Repeat for 0.20 m/s.
steps: Convert diameter: D = 50 mm = 0.05 m. Kinematic viscosity ν = 1.0×10⁻⁶ m²/s.
Re = 3000 lies between 2000 and 4000, so the flow is transitional.
Re = 10000 is above 4000, so the flow is turbulent.
examples.answer: At 0.06 m/s, Re = 3000 and the flow is transitional; at 0.20 m/s, Re = 10000 and the flow is turbulent.

traps: Using pipe radius in place of diameter. Re uses D, the full diameter. A 50 mm pipe has D = 0.05 m, not 0.025 m.
Mixing μ and ν. μ is dynamic viscosity in Pa·s; ν = μ/ρ is kinematic viscosity in m²/s. Use the formula that matches the data.
Forgetting unit conversion. Convert mm to m before dividing by ν in m²/s.
Treating Re = 2000 as an exact switch. The critical zone is about 2000 to 4000; disturbances shift the change.
Giving units to Re. It is dimensionless; do not write Re = 3000 m/s.

quiz.q: Write the Reynolds number for pipe flow in terms of ρ, V, D and μ, and state its units.
quiz.a: Re = ρVD/μ. It has no units.

quiz.q: State the common lower and upper critical Reynolds numbers for pipe flow.
quiz.a: Lower critical Re ≈ 2000; upper critical Re ≈ 4000.

quiz.q: Why does the dye thread blur in turbulent flow but stay straight in laminar flow?
quiz.a: In laminar flow, particles stay in layers and the dye stays in one layer. In turbulent flow, eddies mix fluid across the pipe, so the dye spreads into a cloud.

quiz.q: Show that Re = ρVD/μ is dimensionless.
quiz.a: ρVD has units (kg/m³)(m/s)(m) = kg/(m·s). μ has units Pa·s = kg/(m·s). The units cancel.

quiz.q: Oil with ρ = 850 kg/m³ and μ = 0.12 Pa·s flows at V = 0.9 m/s in a pipe of D = 80 mm. Find Re and classify the flow.
Water (ν = 1.0×10⁻⁶ m²/s) flows in a 25 mm pipe. Find the velocities at Re = 2000 and Re = 4000.
In a 40 mm water pipe (ν = 1.0×10⁻⁶ m²/s), a dye line is straight at V = 0.02 m/s. Predict the dye shape at V = 0.8 m/s and support it with Re.
quiz.a: At 0.02 m/s, Re = 0.02 × 0.04 / 1.0×10⁻⁶ = 800, laminar, straight dye. At 0.8 m/s, Re = 0.8 × 0.04 / 1.0×10⁻⁶ = 32000, turbulent; the dye will break into a mixing cloud.

beyond: Not for the exam. Reynolds number is used in microfluidics, where channels are small and Re is often below 1. Blood flow in arteries can be transitional during peak systole. HVAC and pipeline design use Re to choose pumps and to avoid vibration. Search for 'pipe flow transition', 'Reynolds number microfluidics' or 'critical Reynolds number pipe'.
